newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania right eyes power in elections.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania right eyes power in elections.

text.p: Lithuania's resurgent right wing, which spearheaded an anti-Soviet uprising five years ago, is set to oust ruling former Communists in the first round of parliamentary elections at the weekend.
Commentators forecast the election will be an inconclusive victory for Lithuania's most famous citizen, independence leader Vytautas Landsbergis.

Landsbergis, a former music teacher, put Lithuania's independence movement on the map in January 1991. Thirteen people died when Soviet troops seized the television tower in Vilnius, a centre of the anti-Soviet movement.
Although Landsbergis's rightwing Homeland Union is expected to dominate in the two rounds of voting, commentators see a considerable amount of haggling before a new government can be formed.

In the second election since Lithuania regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, the Homeland Union is facing off against the ex-Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
The first round of voting takes place on Sunday, with a runoff on November 10.
Lithuanians have so far shown little enthusiasm for the election with many undecided and some analysts predict fringe parties may receive more support than usual.
President Algirdas Brazauskas, head of the LDLP before becoming president in 1993, said he would vote for stability.
"Revolutionary changes occur only in politically and democratically immature countries," Brazauskas, now without party affiliation, told a news conference.

The LDLP 1992 election victory shocked many as Landsbergis was most closely linked with Lithuania's independence drive. It also began a trend in eastern Europe as former Communists made political comebacks.
The LDLP has made economic gains and been applauded by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) despite coming to power on a populist platform of easing the pain of reforms.
But many people are disillusioned with the party, criticising it for corruption and croneyism.
It was badly discredited by a banking crisis at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his personal savings from a bank days before it was shut.
Commentators say winning an outright majority will not be plain sailing for the Homeland Union and foresee Lithuania heading for its first coalition government.
Many expect the Homeland Union to be the largest party in the 141-seat parliament and ally with the Christian Democrats, who stress "traditional values" in a nation where Roman Catholicism is strong.
The Homeland Union will have to look for support among other parties likely to enter parliament, the Farmers Union, Womens Party and the Liberal Union, analysts said.
